title: Tria capita ex opere quodam majori inedito de theoria lunae

deep.reconstruction:
Context (from §§12-14 on the previous page): Euler wants the true place of the lunar node and the true inclination of the lunar orbit from the timings of a total lunar eclipse, here that of 1722. For each of the four contacts the geometry gives an expression for sin²(ρ/2), where ρ is an unknown angle:
- first and last contact use the outer shadow radius f together with the auxiliary arcs a and b;
- beginning and end of totality use the inner radius F together with A and B.
The unknowns are two arcs x and y, essentially the Moon's distances from the node at two reference instants, with y ≈ x − c. Each formula has the form
  sin²(ρ/2) = −sin½(x−y ± (a−b) − f)·sin½(x−y ± (a−b) + f) / [sin(y ∓ a)·sin(x ∓ b)],
and similarly with A, B, F. Since all four values must be equal, this gives three equations in the two unknowns.

Euler avoids eliminating one unknown because the result would be too complicated. Instead he uses a two-variable 'regula falsi'. He evaluates the formulas at three trial points:
- I: ½(x−y)=38'', ½(x+y)=4°16'0'';
- II: (x+y)/2 lowered by 5';
- III: (x−y)/2 lowered by 10''.
He then interpolates linearly to the values that make the expressions equal. In modern terms this is a secant / linear-interpolation step on a 2×2 nonlinear system.

This page lists the twelve evaluated fractions (4 formulas × 3 hypotheses). The interpolation yields a correction p = 102'' to ½(x−y). That would make ½(x−y) negative, i.e. y > x, which is physically inadmissible.

§15 diagnoses the cause. Besides the uncertainty of the contact times, the Earth's shadow is effectively larger than the geometric one. Atmospheric refraction actually shortens the umbral cone so that its apex does not reach the Moon. Even so, the atmosphere at such grazing path lengths is so opaque that it acts like an opaque shell. The shadow semidiameter should therefore be increased in the ratio of atmospheric height to Earth's radius. Taking 12 (German) miles from twilight observations and a radius of 860 miles gives about 1/71. Applied to the semidiameter 44'40'' this is +38''. Hence f and F each increase by 38'', and the half-angles in the numerators by 19''.

§16: recomputing with the 19'' correction reduces the absurdity but does not remove it. Everything is consistent if the correction is 30''. That means the atmosphere must act as opaque up to about 20 miles, 'more than half again' the twilight height. His conclusion is that, because the true size of the shadow is unknown, eclipses cannot fix the node and inclination better than the tables already do. One should keep the tabular elements until precise observations of maximum or vanishing lunar latitude are available.

A new chapter then begins on apparent diameters and hourly motions of Sun and Moon in lunar eclipses. It uses the solar orbit with e = 0.0167595, Kepler's equation U = V + e sin V (anomalies counted from apogee) and dθ = dV·√(1−e²)/(1+e cos V).
errors: Terminology slip in §16. In §15 an atmospheric layer of 12 miles corresponds to +38'' in the shadow semidiameter and +19'' in the numerator half-angles. In §16 'semidiameter umbrae 19'' augeatur' and '30'' augeatur' must refer to the half-angles. Otherwise the 30'' case (smaller than 38'') could not correspond to a thicker atmosphere of ~20 miles. Read as half-angles, 30'' means +60'' in the semidiameter, i.e. 12·60/38 ≈ 19 ≈ 20 miles, which is consistent.
Minor: 860/12 = 71.7, so the stated 1/71 is a rounding; 2680''/71.7 ≈ 37.4'', given as 38''. The approximation is acceptable.
The previous page announced trial steps of 10' in x and y. The table actually uses a 10'' change in (x−y)/2 and a 5' change in (x+y)/2. This is internally consistent with §14 but differs from §12.

I spot-checked all twelve fractions against a=1°2'22'', b=4'11'', f=1°1'17'', A=19'48'', B=1'20'', F=28'2'' and the x, y of §14. Every argument checks, e.g. y−a = 4°15'22''−1°2'22'' = 3°13'0'' and x+B = 4°17'58''.

ideas.what: Solving an overdetermined pair of transcendental equations for the node distances by three trial hypotheses and linear interpolation (two-dimensional regula falsi), avoiding elimination
ideas.modern_name: multivariate secant / regula falsi (linear interpolation in two unknowns)
ideas.usually_credited_to: traditional (double false position); multivariate secant methods are usually discussed from the 18th–19th c. onward (Gauss, later Wolfe 1959)
ideas.where_published: Euler uses trial-hypothesis interpolation in many astronomical papers on orbits; specifics unsure

ideas.what: Enlargement of the Earth's umbra in lunar eclipses because of the atmosphere, treating the low atmosphere as opaque; correction proportional to atmospheric height over Earth radius
ideas.modern_name: atmospheric enlargement of the Earth's shadow (Lahire / Chauvenet / Danjon rules)
ideas.usually_credited_to: La Hire (1707), later the 1/50 rule associated with Chauvenet and the 1/85 rule with Danjon
ideas.where_published: unsure; the topic was standard in 18th-c. eclipse computation

ideas.what: Empirical estimate that the effective opaque atmosphere must reach about 20 German miles (an increase of about 1' in the shadow semidiameter, roughly 1/45) to reconcile the 1722 eclipse contacts
ideas.usually_credited_to: La Hire's ~1' increase; Mayer's and others' fractional rules

ideas.what: Methodological conclusion that eclipse timings cannot determine node and inclination better than the tables because the shadow size is uncertain; latitude observations are recommended instead
ideas.modern_name: parameter degeneracy / identifiability (shadow radius correlated with node and inclination)

ideas.what: Solar elements for the next chapter: Kepler's equation with anomaly from apogee and the true-anomaly differential
ideas.where_published: numerous Euler papers on solar and lunar theory

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a carefully executed but routine computation: a regula-falsi solution for node distances, plus a discussion of atmospheric enlargement of the Earth's shadow that was standard after La Hire. The one mildly interesting point is Euler's frank negative result. Fitting the 1722 eclipse forces the opaque atmosphere to about 20 miles (≈1' added to the shadow semidiameter), and he concludes eclipses cannot improve the tabular node and inclination. This is a nice documented example of recognizing parameter degeneracy, but not a new mathematical result.
transcription_corrections: None of substance; the fractions and numbers in the transcription agree with the image and check numerically.
§16 'semidiameter umbrae 19'' / 30'' augeatur' is correctly transcribed; the inconsistency is in Euler's wording, not the transcription.
